title: Kshama, forbearance
hook: the Gita lists forgiveness among the divine qualities (Bhagavad Gita 16.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was idfa': push harm back with something better than what came. Your line was a door opening where a wall stood.

A word turns up in a list, an odd place to meet something so hard to do. In the sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna about two kinds of nature a person can be born to, one he calls divine and one demonic. He names the divine qualities first, one after another, like things packed for a long journey. Fearlessness. Purity of heart. Generosity. Self-control. Truthfulness. Freedom from anger. And near the end of the list, in the third verse, kshama.
screen: `A WORD IN A LIST.` → `THE DIVINE QUALITIES.` → `NEAR THE END: KSHAMA.`

segments.voice: Look at its neighbors. In the same verse, right beside kshama, are vigor and fortitude, the strength to keep going under pressure. A little earlier comes freedom from anger. Forgiveness here keeps strong company. It isn't among the soft extras; it's packed in with the steel. Kshama is translated forgiveness, and also forbearance or patience: the capacity to bear what's done to you without striking back. Less a single act after a fight, more a settled way of holding wrongs as they come. Then the setting. Krishna says this on a battlefield, to a man about to go to war. So the Gita isn't describing someone with no enemies, sitting somewhere peaceful. It's describing a person who may have to act, even firmly, and still carries forbearance inside. Hindu teachers read that tension in different ways, and the Gita leaves room for them. Last, whose quality it is. Kshama is listed as a mark of the one who forgives. Nothing in the verse makes it wait on the other person's apology, or on their deserving it. It's part of a divine nature, and some teachers read the list as something a person can grow into. That turns the usual question around. Not, have they earned my forgiveness? But, what kind of nature am I growing?
screen: `STRONG NEIGHBORS IN THE LIST.` · `FORGIVENESS AND FORBEARANCE.` · `SPOKEN ON A BATTLEFIELD.` · `A MARK OF THE ONE WHO FORGIVES.` · then, large: `KSHAMA.`

segments.voice: Picture a moment later today when someone is likely to irritate you, a driver, a coworker, a slow line, and feel the small heat that comes with it. Now picture bearing it: not pretending it's fine, just letting it arrive and pass through without striking back, breathing out slowly as if making room. If you pray, you can ask for kshama in your own tradition's words.
Kshama. Sanskrit for forgiveness and forbearance, listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita, beside vigor and fortitude. Today's word.
Your line: packed in with the steel. Forbearance takes strength, not softness. Day nine hundred sixty-one, done.

howItsDone: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's list of divine qualities in chapter 16 as a picture of the character to grow toward, and kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is taught as one of them.

notes: Gita 16.1–3 paraphrased (Arnold 1885 is public domain but the writer isn't certain of its exact wording). Qualities named in the hook: abhayam (fearlessness), sattva-samshuddhi (purity of heart), danam (generosity), damah (self-control), satyam (truthfulness), akrodhah (freedom from anger); 16.3 has tejas, kshama, dhriti, shaucham, adroha, natimanita. Confirm 'right beside it' for tejas and dhriti.
'Divine' and 'demonic' (daivi, asuri sampad) per 16.5–6; confirm 'born to'.
'Hindu teachers read that tension in different ways' is deliberately unspecific; a Keeper may add named readings.
Editor pass: the hook now follows the chapter's order (divine qualities named first); 'something a person can grow into' and 'doesn't wait on an apology' marked as readings, not the verse's words.
